summary: Specifies how to use Datagram Transport Layer Security over DCCP. DTLS gives privacy and tamper detection to datagram applications, and DCCP provides a congestion-controlled but unreliable datagram service. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: DCCP is a datagram transport that slows the sender down when the network is busy. DTLS is the encrypted, tamper-detecting version of TLS that works over unreliable datagrams. This RFC says how to run DTLS over DCCP: the encrypted records ride inside DCCP data packets, and the two setup conversations happen one after the other.

questions: how does dtls work with dccp
what is a dccp service code
subtitle: Putting encryption on a datagram transport that also controls congestion.

tldr.problem: DCCP gives applications a datagram service with congestion control, and DTLS gives datagram applications privacy and tamper detection, but there was no way to run the two together.
tldr.mechanism: DTLS records are carried in the payload of DCCP-Data packets, one or more per packet and never split across packets. The two connection handshakes run one after the other, with an option to overlap them.
tldr.outcome: The combination was standardised, with rules for the handshake timers, for the interaction with congestion control, and for the packet size limit that the two protocols each maintain.

facts.label: DTLS records per DCCP packet
facts.value: One or more, each wholly inside one packet

today: RFC 5238 is a Proposed Standard and is listed as updated by RFC 8996, which deprecates TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1. The document is short by design and, as it says itself, it is assumed to apply to all future versions of DTLS unless a change to DTLS or DCCP makes the encapsulation need revising.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document specifies how to carry application payloads with Datagram Transport Layer Security in the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol.

DTLS is an adaptation of Transport Layer Security that modifies TLS for use with the unreliable transport protocol UDP. TLS is a protocol that allows client and server applications to communicate in a way that is designed to prevent eavesdropping and to detect tampering and message forgery. DTLS can be viewed as TLS plus adaptations for unreliability.

DCCP provides an unreliable transport service similar to UDP, but with adaptive congestion control similar to TCP and SCTP. DCCP can be viewed equally well as either UDP plus congestion control or TCP minus reliability, although, unlike TCP, DCCP offers multiple congestion control algorithms.

The combination of DTLS and DCCP offers transport security capabilities to applications using DCCP similar to those available for TCP, UDP and SCTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Two protocols with different jobs. DTLS hides the content of messages and makes sure nobody tampers with them. DCCP keeps the sending rate in step with what the network can carry. This RFC is about running one on top of the other.

sections.title: How DTLS Records Travel in DCCP
sections.content:
The approach is very straightforward: DTLS records are transmitted in the application data fields of DCCP-Data and DCCP-DataAck packets, and in the rest of the document a DCCP-Data packet means a DCCP-Data or a DCCP-DataAck packet.

Multiple DTLS records may be sent in one DCCP-Data packet, as long as the resulting packet is within the path maximum transfer unit currently in force for normal data packets if fragmentation is not allowed, meaning the Don't Fragment bit is set for IPv4 or no fragmentation extension headers are used for IPv6, or within the current DCCP maximum packet size if fragmentation is allowed. A single DTLS record must be fully contained in a single DCCP-Data packet, and must not be split over multiple packets.

DCCP and DTLS both use sequence numbers in their packets and records, but those sequence numbers serve somewhat, but not completely, overlapping functions. Consequently there is no connection between the sequence number of a DCCP packet and the sequence number in a DTLS record contained in that packet, and no connection between sequence number related features such as DCCP synchronisation and DTLS anti-replay protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Each encrypted record is a unit that travels whole: it goes inside one DCCP packet and is never cut in half. Several records may share a packet, but never the other way round. The two protocols number their packets separately and their counters have nothing to do with each other.

sections.title: The Two Handshakes
sections.content:
Unlike UDP, DCCP is connection-oriented and has a connection handshake procedure that precedes the transmission of data packets. DTLS is also connection-oriented and has a handshake procedure of its own that must precede the transmission of actual application information. Because DTLS records map onto DCCP data packets, the two handshakes are forced to happen in series, with the DCCP handshake first and the DTLS handshake following, which is how TLS over TCP works.

However, the DCCP handshake packets DCCP-Request and DCCP-Response have application data fields and can carry user data during the DCCP handshake, and this creates the opportunity to perform the handshakes partially in parallel. A DTLS client may choose to transmit one or more DTLS records, typically containing DTLS handshake messages or parts of them, in the DCCP-Request packet. A DTLS server may process these records as usual and, if it has records to send in response, include them in the DCCP-Response packet, or it may delay the response until the DCCP handshake completes and then send the DTLS response in a DCCP-Data packet.

Even though the DCCP handshake is a reliable process, with DCCP handshake messages retransmitted as required if messages are lost, the transfer of application data in DCCP-Request and DCCP-Response packets is not necessarily reliable. A DCCP server is free to discard application data received in DCCP-Request packets, and if a request or response needs to be retransmitted the DCCP implementation may choose not to include the application data present in the initial message.

Because the next opportunity to send data after sending data in a DCCP-Request is only after the connection handshake completes, the only way for DTLS to retransmit records that were originally transmitted in DCCP-Request or DCCP-Response packets is to wait for the DCCP handshake to complete and then resend the records in DCCP-Data packets.

DCCP and DTLS use similar strategies for retransmitting handshake messages. If there is no response to the original request within normally 1 second, the message is retransmitted, the timer is then doubled and the process repeated until a response is received or a maximum time is exceeded. Therefore, if DTLS records are sent in a DCCP-Request packet and that packet or the response is lost, the two handshakes could time out on similar schedules. To avoid multiple DTLS retransmissions queuing up before the first retransmission can be sent, DTLS over DCCP must wait until the completion of the DCCP handshake before restarting its DTLS handshake retransmission timer.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the connection is set up first and the encryption is negotiated second. But the first DCCP packet can already carry the start of the encrypted handshake, so the two conversations can partly overlap. The rule that matters: DTLS must not start counting out its own handshake again until DCCP has finished its handshake.

sections.title: Congestion Control and the Handshake
sections.content:
Given the large potential sizes of the DTLS handshake messages, it is possible that DCCP congestion control could throttle the transmission of the DTLS handshake to the point that the transfer cannot complete before the DTLS timeout and retransmission procedures take effect. Adding retransmitted messages to a congested situation might only make matters worse and delay connection establishment. A DTLS over UDP application transmitting handshake data into the same network situation will not necessarily receive better throughput and might actually see worse effective throughput, since without the pacing of slow-start and congestion control a UDP application might be making congestion worse and lowering the effective throughput it receives. As the DTLS specification says, mishandling of the retransmission timer can lead to serious congestion problems.

DTLS over DCCP implementations should take steps to avoid retransmitting a request that has been queued but not yet actually transmitted by DCCP, when the underlying DCCP implementation can provide this information. For example, DTLS could delay starting the retransmission timer until DCCP indicates the message has been transferred from DCCP to the IP layer.

If the throughput needs of the actual application data differ from the needs of the DTLS handshake, the handshake transfer could leave the DCCP congestion control in a state that is not immediately suitable for the application data that will follow. DCCP Congestion Control Identifier 2 congestion control uses an Additive Increase Multiplicative Decrease algorithm similar to TCP congestion control, and if it is used then transferring a large handshake could cause a multiplicative decrease that would not have happened with the application data. The application might then be throttled while waiting for additive increase to return throughput to acceptable levels.

Applications where this might be a problem should consider using DCCP Congestion Control Identifier 3, which implements TCP-Friendly Rate Control. TFRC varies the allowed throughput more slowly than the additive increase and multiplicative decrease algorithm and might avoid the discontinuities possible with CCID 2.
sections.plainLanguage: The setup conversation can be slowed down by the very congestion control meant to protect the network, so that the handshake times out and starts again, making things worse. And a slow start during the handshake can leave the connection at a low sending rate afterwards.

sections.title: Sessions, Connections and Their Relationship
sections.content:
DTLS uses the concepts of sessions and connections. A DTLS connection is used by upper-layer endpoints to exchange data over a transport protocol. DTLS sessions contain cached state information used to reduce the number of roundtrips and the computation required to create multiple DTLS connections between the same endpoints.

In DTLS over DCCP, a DTLS connection is carried by a DCCP connection. Often the DCCP connection establishment is immediately followed by DTLS connection establishment, either creating a new DTLS session with a full handshake or resuming an existing one, and the DTLS connection termination is immediately followed by DCCP connection termination, but that is not the only possibility. The life of a DTLS over DCCP connection is completely contained within the life of the underlying DCCP connection, and a DTLS connection cannot continue if its underlying DCCP connection terminates. However, multiple DTLS connections can be resumed from the same DTLS session, each running over its own DCCP connection. The session resumption features of DTLS are widely used, so this situation is likely to occur in many use cases.

It is possible for an application to start a DCCP connection by transferring unprotected packets and then switch to DTLS after some time, which is likely to be useful for applications that would like to negotiate using DTLS or not, and it has implications for the choice of DCCP service code.

Many DTLS application programming interfaces do not prevent an application from sending a mix of encrypted and clear packets over the same transport connection. Applications must not send unprotected data on a DCCP connection while it is also carrying a DTLS connection, since that presents a vulnerability to packet insertion attacks.

Many DTLS APIs also allow an application to start multiple DTLS connections over one transport connection in series, with the termination of one followed by the start of another. Processing a DTLS handshake is relatively CPU intensive, so an application that uses this strategy is open to an attacker who repeatedly starts and immediately stops sessions. Applications that use this strategy should limit the potential burden on the system by some means, for example by enforcing a minimum time of 1 second between session initiations.
sections.plainLanguage: An encrypted connection cannot outlive the DCCP connection under it. But the same cached encryption state can be reused on a fresh DCCP connection, which saves a full handshake. Two cautions: never mix clear and encrypted packets on one connection, and do not let an attacker start and stop sessions as fast as they like.

sections.title: Path MTU Discovery
sections.content:
Each DTLS record must fit within a single DCCP-Data packet. DCCP packets are normally transmitted with the Don't Fragment bit set for IPv4, or without fragmentation extension headers for IPv6, and because of this DCCP performs path maximum transmission unit discovery.

DTLS also normally uses the Don't Fragment bit and performs path MTU discovery on its own, using an algorithm strongly similar to the one used by DCCP. A DTLS over DCCP implementation may use the DCCP-managed value for the MTU and not perform discovery on its own. However, implementations that choose to use the DCCP-managed value should continue to follow the DTLS procedures with regard to fragmenting handshake messages during handshake retransmissions. Alternatively, an implementation may choose to use its own discovery calculations but must not use a value greater than the value determined by DCCP.

DTLS implementations normally allow applications to reset the MTU estimate back to the initial state, and when that happens DTLS over DCCP implementations should also reset the DCCP MTU estimation. DTLS implementations also sometimes allow applications to control the use of the Don't Fragment bit when running over IPv4, or the use of fragmentation extension headers when running over IPv6, and DTLS over DCCP implementations should control those in concert with the application's indications when the DCCP implementation supports it.

The DCCP Maximum Packet Size is bounded by the current congestion control state, the Congestion Control Maximum Packet Size. Even when the Don't Fragment bit is not set and DCCP packets may then be fragmented, the Maximum Packet Size may be less than the 65,535 bytes normally used in UDP. It is also possible for the Congestion Control Maximum Packet Size, and thus the Maximum Packet Size, to vary over time as congestion conditions change. DTLS over DCCP implementations must not use a DTLS record size greater than the DCCP Maximum Packet Size currently in force.
sections.plainLanguage: The size limit is set by DCCP, not by DTLS, and it moves with the congestion state, so it can be smaller than the usual UDP limit. An implementation that keeps its own estimate must never exceed the one DCCP has worked out.

sections.title: DCCP Service Codes and New DTLS Versions
sections.content:
The DCCP connection handshake includes a field called the Service Code, intended to describe the application-level service the client wants to connect to. Service codes provide information about which application protocol a connection intends to use, thus aiding middleboxes and reducing reliance on globally well-known ports.

It is expected that many middleboxes will give different privileges to applications running DTLS over DCCP than to applications running plain DCCP. Applications that use DTLS over DCCP sometimes and plain DCCP other times should register and use different service codes for each mode of operation. Applications that use both DCCP and DTLS over DCCP may choose to listen for incoming connections on the same DCCP port and distinguish the mode of the request by the offered service code. Some applications may start out using DCCP without DTLS and then optionally switch to using DTLS over the same connection; since there is no way to change the service code for a connection after it is established, these applications will use one service code.

As DTLS matures, revisions to its specification can be expected. DTLS includes mechanisms for identifying the version in use, and presumably future versions will either include backward compatibility modes or at least not allow connections between dissimilar versions. Since DTLS over DCCP simply encapsulates the DTLS records transparently, these changes should not affect this document, and in the absence of a revision to it the document is assumed to apply to all future versions of DTLS. It will only be revised if a revision to DTLS or DCCP, including its related congestion control identifiers, makes a revision to the encapsulation necessary.

It is recommended that an application migrating to a new version of DTLS keep the same DCCP service code used for the old version and allow DTLS to provide the version negotiation support. If a new version of DTLS provides significant new capabilities to the application that could change the behaviour of middleboxes, an application developer may register a new service code.
sections.plainLanguage: The service code is a label in the connection setup that says what the connection is for, which is what lets a firewall treat encrypted and unencrypted traffic differently. It cannot be changed later, so an application that starts unprotected and later switches to encrypted has to pick one label for the whole connection.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security considerations for DTLS are specified in the DTLS specification and for DCCP in the DCCP specification. The combination of DTLS and DCCP introduces no new security considerations.

The security points made elsewhere in the document remain in force. Applications must not send unprotected data on a DCCP connection that is also carrying a DTLS connection, because that presents a vulnerability to packet insertion attacks, and an application that repeatedly starts and immediately stops DTLS sessions should limit the burden it places on the system.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is introduced by putting the two together. The security rules of each protocol still apply, including the rule against mixing clear and encrypted packets on one connection.

viz.caption: WHERE CONGESTION CONTROL AND THE HANDSHAKE GET IN THE WAY

items.title: The handshake can be throttled
items.text: Congestion control may slow the handshake so much that it times out, and the retransmissions make the congestion worse.

items.title: Do not start the timer too early
items.text: Delay the DTLS retransmission timer until DCCP says the message has actually left for the IP layer.

items.title: Mishandling the timer is dangerous
items.text: The DTLS specification warns that mishandling the retransmission timer can lead to serious congestion problems.

items.title: The rate may stay low afterwards
items.text: With CCID 2 a large handshake can trigger a multiplicative decrease that the application data alone would not have caused.

items.title: CCID 3 changes the shape
items.text: CCID 3 uses TCP-Friendly Rate Control, which varies the allowed throughput more slowly and may avoid the discontinuity.

viz.caption: THREE WAYS TO HANDLE THE PACKET SIZE LIMIT
